lead.t: | Hypoparathyroidism | Hypocalcaemia, low PTH, high phosphate | Low PTH is the hallmark; postoperative neck surgery common cause. |

b: ↓PTH → hypocalcaemia + hyperphosphataemia.

Causes: Post-surgical ( 1), autoimmune APS-1 (AIRE mutation — candidiasis + hypoparathyroidism + adrenal insufficiency), DiGeorge (22q11 deletion — absent parathyroids + thymic aplasia + cardiac defects), hypomagnesaemia.

Clinical: Tetany — circumoral tingling, carpopedal spasm, laryngospasm, generalised seizures. Chvostek's sign (tap facial nerve → facial twitch). Trousseau's sign (BP cuff → carpal spasm — most specific). Prolonged QT on ECG, cataracts, bas
Treatment: Acute → IV calcium gluconate. Chronic → oral calcium + calcitriol.

snip.t: | Hypoparathyroidism | Hypocalcaemia, low PTH, high phosphate | Low PTH is the hallmark; postoperative neck surgery common cause. |
| Pseudohypoparathyroidism | Hypocalcaemia, high PTH, short stature, brachydactyly | End‑organ resistance to PTH; PTH is elevated, unlike true hypoparathyroidism. |
Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis is most often the first manifestation of APS-1, followed by hypoparathyroidism and then by Addison disease, which typically develops in early adolescence.
In children, hypoparathyroidism is the most commonly associated disorder, and it is suspected if hypocalcemia and elevated phosphate levels are present.
It is classically characterized by the triad of mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and primary adrenal insufficiency.
Complications of surgical treatment are rare and include hypoparathyroidism (transient or permanent) and paralysis of the vocal cords.

Note the raised phosphate (1.8 mmol/L, above reference 0.8–1.4) — this is a genuine abnormality requiring clinical correlation; possible causes include hypoparathyroidism, renal tubular dysfunction, or excess dietary phosphate.

qs.q: A patient with hypoparathyroidism is prescribed calcitriol. Which pharmacokinetic property is most relevant to its use?
o: Undergoes rapid metabolic degradation in hepatic tissue.
Shows extensive binding to plasma proteins in circulation.
Functions as the fully active form of vitamin D.
Is primarily excreted as metabolites via the kidneys.
Is efficiently absorbed through the gastric mucosa.
qs.e: Calcitriol is the active form of vitamin D, bypassing the need for renal hydroxylation.

qs.q: A patient with autoimmune hypoparathyroidism exhibits profound neuromuscular irritability and painful carpopedal spasms. Which underlying physiological process is directly disrupted by the low ionized calcium?
qs.e: Hypocalcemia reduces the shielding of extracellular negative surface charges, lowering the threshold for neuronal membrane depolarization.

qs.q: DiGeorge syndrome caused by a 22q11.2 deletion leads to hypoparathyroidism primarily through which mechanism?
o: Autoimmune destruction affecting both of the developing parathyroid glands
Activating mutations of the calcium-sensing receptor inhibiting PTH release
Surgical removal of the parathyroid glands during complex cardiac surgery
Failure of normal embryonic development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches
qs.e: DiGeorge syndrome involves abnormal development of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches, resulting in absent or hypoplastic parathyroid glands and thymic hypoplasia. This leads to neonatal hypocalcemia and T-cell deficiency.

qs.q: A 30-year-old female is investigated for hypercalcaemia. In primary hypoparathyroidism, which paired laboratory derangement of calcium and phosphate is characteristically found?
qs.e: Hypoparathyroidism results in hypocalcaemia due to a lack of parathyroid hormone-mediated bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption, coupled with hyperphosphataemia from decreased renal phosphate excretion. Hyperparathyroidism would show the opposite pattern of high calcium and low phosphate.

qs.q: The most common cause of hypoparathyroidism is
o: Inadvertent surgical removal during thyroidectomy or neck surgery
qs.e: Surgical hypoparathyroidism is most common — inadvertent removal or devascularization of parathyroids during total thyroidectomy, parathyroidectomy, or radical neck dissection. Presents within hours to days post-op with hypocalcemia → perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm, tetany, seizures.

qs.q: Autosomal dominant hypoparathyroidism is caused by mutations in
qs.e: Gain-of-function CASR mutations → receptor is hypersensitive to calcium → PTH suppressed even at normal/low calcium levels → hypocalcemia + hypercalciuria. Autosomal dominant. Treat cautiously — vitamin D/calcium supplementation worsens hypercalciuria and can cause nephrocalcinosis.

qs.q: Familial isolated hypoparathyroidism (FIH) is linked to mutations in
o: Mutations in the cyclin D1 gene
qs.e: GCM2 is a transcription factor essential for parathyroid gland development. Loss-of-function mutations → absent/hypoplastic parathyroids → isolated hypoparathyroidism (no other endocrine deficiencies, unlike APS-1 or DiGeorge). Can be autosomal dominant or recessive.

qs.q: 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge syndrome) causes hypoparathyroidism due to
qs.e: DiGeorge: 22q11.2 deletion → TBX1 gene haploinsufficiency → failed 3rd/4th pharyngeal pouch development → absent parathyroids (hypocalcemia/tetany) + absent thymus (T-cell immunodeficiency) + conotruncal cardiac defects. CATCH-22: Cardiac defects, Abnormal facies, Thymic hypoplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcemia, 22q11.

ai.title: Hypoparathyroidism
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Low parathyroid hormone causes hypocalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia. In low‑resource settings postoperative neck surgery, autoimmune disease and magnesium deficiency are common causes.

sections.p: Hypoparathyroidism is defined by inappropriately low serum PTH in the presence of hypocalcaemia (corrected Ca <2.1 mmol/L) and hyperphosphataemia (>1.4 mmol/L).
b: Low PTH is the hallmark
Serum calcium, phosphate, magnesium and PTH must be measured together

sections.p: Severity is graded by serum calcium and symptom burden:
b: Mild: Ca 2.0‑2.1 mmol/L, no tetany
Moderate: Ca 1.8‑2.0 mmol/L, intermittent paresthesia or positive Chvostek/Trousseau
Severe: Ca <1.8 mmol/L, tetany, seizures, laryngospasm, prolonged QT

sections.p: In East African and other low‑resource hospitals the common aetiologies are:
b: Post‑surgical removal or damage of parathyroids (thyroidectomy, neck dissection)
Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 (candidiasis, adrenal insufficiency)
DiGeorge syndrome (22q11 deletion) – rare but important in young patients
Severe hypomagnesaemia from diarrhoea, malnutrition or chronic alcoholism
Rare: infiltrative disease (hemochromatosis, sarcoidosis), genetic mutations (CASR, GCM2)

sections.p: Patients develop signs of acute hypocalcaemia and chronic complications.
b: Perioral tingling, carpopedal spasm, painful muscle cramps
Positive Chvostek’s sign (facial twitch on tapping)
Positive Trousseau’s sign (carpal spasm with cuff inflation) – most specific
Seizures, laryngospasm, bronchospasm in severe cases
Prolonged QT interval on ECG, cataracts, basal ganglia calcifications on CT

t.b: Confirms hypocalcaemia; guides urgency of treatment
Elevated in true hypoparathyroidism; helps differentiate from pseudohypoparathyroidism
Low or undetectable confirms diagnosis; high PTH suggests resistance
Low magnesium can suppress PTH secretion; correct before calcium replacement
Looks for prolonged QT; if unavailable, monitor for arrhythmia clinically
Guides calcium carbonate use and monitors for nephrocalcinosis

sections.p: Untreated severe hypocalcaemia can be fatal.
b: Life‑threatening tetany or laryngospasm
Seizures or status epilepticus
Cardiac arrhythmias from prolonged QT
Nephrocalcinosis and renal insufficiency from overt calcium‑vitamin D therapy

sections.p: Treat the acute deficit, then maintain long‑term calcium‑vitamin D balance while addressing the underlying cause.
b: Acute: IV calcium gluconate 10 % (if IV line available) – monitor cardiac rhythm
Magnesium repletion (IV/PO magnesium sulfate) before calcium if Mg <0.7 mmol/L
Avoid thiazide diuretics that raise calcium excretion; avoid high‑dose vitamin D that can cause hypercalciuria

sections.p: Regular monitoring prevents complications and guides dose adjustments.
b: Check serum calcium, phosphate, magnesium and creatinine every 3–6 months
Annual ECG for QT interval
Renal ultrasound if persistent hypercalciuria or symptoms of nephrolithiasis
Educate patients on signs of tetany and when to seek urgent care
Pseudohypoparathyroidism – high PTH, short stature, brachydactyly; treat with calcium and vitamin D but PTH is elevated
Vitamin D deficiency – low/normal PTH, low phosphate; history of poor sun exposure or diet
Low albumin can falsely lower total calcium – use ionised calcium or correct for albumin
Acute illness can transiently suppress PTH – repeat measurement after stabilisation

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe tetany, laryngospasm or airway compromise
Syncope or palpitations with prolonged QT on ECG

faq.q: Why is phosphate high in hypoparathyroidism?
faq.a: PTH normally promotes renal phosphate excretion; low PTH reduces excretion, causing hyperphosphataemia.

faq.q: Can calcium supplements alone correct the problem?
faq.a: No – without active vitamin D, intestinal calcium absorption remains limited; calcitriol is required.

faq.q: What is the most specific bedside sign?
faq.a: Trousseau’s sign (carpal spasm with cuff inflation) is highly specific for hypocalcaemia.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman presents with perioral tingling after thyroidectomy – what immediate test and treatment do you initiate? — Check ionised calcium and give IV calcium gluconate if <1.8 mmol/L.
How does hypomagnesaemia interfere with the diagnosis of hypoparathyroidism? — Low Mg suppresses PTH release; correct Mg before interpreting PTH levels.
Differentiate true hypoparathyroidism from pseudohypoparathyroidism using labs. — Low PTH = true; high PTH with similar calcium/phosphate = pseudo.
Why is calcitriol preferred over cholecalciferol for chronic management? — Calcitriol bypasses renal 1‑α‑hydroxylation, providing active hormone directly.

A patient on chronic calcium and calcitriol develops renal stones – what adjustment should you consider? — Reduce calcium dose, add thiazide diuretic to lower urinary calcium, monitor 24‑h urine calcium.
Explain the pathophysiological link between prolonged QT and hypocalcaemia. — Low extracellular calcium prolongs phase 2 of ventricular action potential, lengthening QT.
What red‑flag symptom would prompt you to call for emergency airway support? — Sudden laryngospasm or stridor indicating airway obstruction.
In a low‑resource clinic without PTH assay, how can you still diagnose hypoparathyroidism? — Rely on hypocalcaemia, hyperphosphataemia, clinical tetany, and exclusion of vitamin D deficiency.
